title: How To Handle An Angry, Verbally Aggressive Student e-student/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin outlines how teachers should respond to emotional outbursts, tantrums, and verbal aggression, distinguishing them from typical rule-breaking. He first lists what not to do: immediately enforcing a consequence, getting angry, touching the student, or attempting conversation, all of which risk escalating the situation. His recommended approach is to stay calm, observe from a safe distance, shield other students from involvement, often do or say nothing at all, use brief calming language only if necessary, and wait until the student is fully calm before addressing the incident. Afterward, teachers should document what happened, contact parents with facts rather than opinions, hold the student accountable once calm with a stiffened consequence, and generally handle the matter themselves rather than involving administration unless the behavior turns physically aggressive. Linsin emphasizes that patience and observation, rather than immediate intervention, best establish the teacher as being in control.
points: Do not immediately enforce a consequence, get angry, touch the student, or attempt conversation during an angry outburst—all risk escalation.
Stay calm, observe from a safe distance, and shield other students from becoming involved in the incident.
Wait until the student is fully calm—potentially a couple of hours—before addressing or discussing the outburst.
Document the incident thoroughly and contact parents with facts only, without offering opinions or conclusions.
Handle severe misbehavior yourself rather than involving administration, unless the behavior becomes physically aggressive.
quotes: Emotional outbursts, temper tantrums, yelling, lashing out. Severe misbehavior like this needs to be dealt with differently than typical rule breaking.
You must hold students who act out in anger accountable—without a doubt—but not right away. You risk escalating the problem if you immediately try to pull them aside or put them in time-out.
It’s common for teachers to place a hand on a student’s shoulder in an attempt to calm. But you don’t know what students are thinking in any given moment or what they’re capable of.
Often, it’s best not to say or do anything. If the angry student stops the behavior, simply continue on with what you were doing—for now—allowing the student time to cool off.
As soon as you are able, document the student’s behavior. Write down everything said or done and interview all students near or involved in the incident.
Unless the behavior is physically aggressive, I’m not in favor of getting the principal involved. Involving administration weakens your authority and your ability to manage your classroom.
